goals: Describe Harappan subsistence strategies and the planning of Mohenjodaro
Infer social differences from burials and artefacts, with the right cautions
Explain how craft centres are identified and how materials were procured
Use evidence to answer short and long questions on Harappan life

slides.heading: Bricks, Beads and Bones
slides.body_md: Part 1: how the **Harappans farmed**, how they planned their towns, and how they made and obtained their goods.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: phases and farming, planning at Mohenjodaro, social differences, craft production, and the procurement of materials
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: The Harappan civilisation flourished more than four thousand years ago, yet we know about it only from what archaeologists dig up. In this part we look at what the Harappans ate, how Mohenjodaro was planned, what burials and objects say about society, and how craft workers found their materials.

visual.caption: Three phases of the Harappan story

slides.narration: Historians speak of three phases. Early Harappan cultures came before about twenty six hundred BCE. The mature phase, with its cities, seals, script and weights, lasted from about twenty six hundred to nineteen hundred BCE. Late Harappan cultures followed. The civilisation is named after Harappa, the first site where its remains were identified.

slides.heading: What the Harappans ate
slides.body_md: Food is traced through **plant remains**, **animal bones**, **tools and fields** and **water works**.

rows: Wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, sesame; millets in Gujarat; rice only rarely
Cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig; wild animals and fish also eaten
Terracotta plough models; a ploughed field at Kalibangan

visual.alt: Table of the kinds of evidence for Harappan food: plant remains such as wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame; animal bones of domestic and wild animals and fish; tools and fields; and water works
visual.caption: How we know what they ate

slides.narration: Burnt grains show that people ate wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame. Millets appear at some Gujarat sites, but rice only rarely. Bones show that cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig were kept, while wild animals and fish were also eaten. Each kind of evidence answers a different question about food.

slides.heading: Fields and water
slides.body_md: Models, fields and water works show **how farming was done**.

rows: Ploughed field, furrows at right angles

visual.alt: Table of farming and water evidence: plough models at Cholistan and Banawali, the ploughed field with furrows at right angles at Kalibangan, canal traces at Shortughai, and reservoirs at Dholavira

slides.narration: Terracotta models of the plough come from Cholistan and Banawali. At Kalibangan, archaeologists found a ploughed field with two sets of furrows at right angles, which may mean that two crops were grown together. Traces of canals were found at Shortughai, and Dholavira had reservoirs. Each is a clue, and none is a complete picture.

visual.caption: Citadel and Lower Town

slides.narration: Mohenjodaro was divided into two parts. The Citadel was smaller and higher, built on platforms of mud brick, and lay to the west. The Lower Town was larger and lower, also walled, and lay to the east. This drawing is a schematic plan, not a map, and it shows only the main idea of the layout.

slides.heading: Planned before it was built
slides.body_md: The platforms and **drains were laid out first**, and the houses were fitted around them.

visual.alt: Flow showing planning before building at Mohenjodaro: platforms laid, drains laid out, standard bricks, then houses built around them
visual.caption: Planned before it was built

slides.narration: Archaeologists conclude that Mohenjodaro was planned before it was built. The mud-brick platforms were laid first, and the drains were laid out before the houses. Bricks followed a standard ratio of four to two to one for length, breadth and height, and the same ratio is found at sites far apart.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Citadel
slides.body_md: Compared with the Lower Town, the Citadel was…
slides.narration: Remember its size, its height and its position.

visual.caption: A courtyard house

slides.narration: Many houses were built around a courtyard, with rooms opening onto it. The wall facing the street often had no windows at ground level, which gave privacy. Bathing rooms had drains that joined the drains of the lane, and many houses had their own wells. The plan shows a settled urban way of life.

slides.heading: The Great Bath and the warehouse
slides.body_md: Two public structures stood on the Citadel. Both names carry **interpretations**.

rows: A water tank with steps, made watertight, in a courtyard on the Citadel
A large building on the Citadel, once called the granary
What was stored is not certain

visual.alt: Table of two public structures on the Citadel: the Great Bath, a watertight tank with steps whose ritual use is an interpretation, and the warehouse, once called the granary, whose contents are not certain

slides.narration: On the Citadel stood the Great Bath, a tank with steps that was made watertight. Many scholars think it was used for special bathing, but that is an interpretation. Another large building was once called the granary and is now often called the warehouse, because what was stored there is not certain.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: planning a 5-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: *Describe the planning of the settlement at Mohenjodaro.*
bullets: Step 1 — One point on the **two parts** of the town.
Step 2 — One point on **platforms laid first**.
Step 3 — One point each on **bricks** and **drains**.
Step 4 — One point on **houses** and public structures.

rows: Two parts: Citadel to the west, Lower Town to the east
Platforms laid first, so the plan came before the building
Standard bricks of one ratio, found at distant sites
Covered drains planned before the houses
Courtyard houses; Great Bath and warehouse as public structures

visual.alt: Table planning a 5-mark answer on Mohenjodaro: one point each on the two parts of the town, platforms laid first, standard bricks, planned drains, and courtyard houses with public structures
visual.caption: Five headed points earn five marks

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a five mark answer. Give one point for the two parts of the town, one for platforms laid first, one for standard bricks and one for planned drains. Use the last mark for courtyard houses and the public structures. Keep each point to about twenty words and write in headed lines.

slides.heading: Quick check: the brick ratio
slides.body_md: Bricks were made in the standard ratio of length to breadth to height of ___.
slides.narration: Think of the same ratio found at distant sites.

slides.heading: Burials and social difference
slides.body_md: Pit burials hint at **some differences**, but the evidence is thin.

rows: Few or no goods in many graves
A few with jewellery or a copper mirror
Goods may reflect belief, not rank
Little display of rank in death
Absence of finds is not proof

visual.alt: Table of burial evidence: pit burials mostly with pottery, a few with jewellery or a copper mirror, and no lavish royal tombs, each with a possible reading and a caution

slides.narration: Most Harappan dead were buried in pits, some with pottery and ornaments, and a few with jewellery or a copper mirror. Grand tombs of rulers have not been found. Historians therefore see hints of social difference but not clear ranks. Beliefs about death also shaped what was buried, so grave goods alone cannot measure wealth.

slides.heading: Utilitarian objects and luxuries
columns: **Utilitarian:** serves daily needs and uses common materials, such as grinding slabs and cooking pots.
**Luxury:** rare materials or costly methods, such as faience vessels and gold ornaments, found mostly in large settlements.

rows: Rare materials or costly methods; not needed daily

visual.alt: Table of two types of artefact: utilitarian objects, which serve daily needs and use common materials, and luxuries, which use rare materials or costly methods; with examples

slides.narration: Archaeologists sort objects into two groups. Utilitarian objects serve daily needs, like grinding slabs and cooking pots. Luxuries are made of rare materials or by costly methods, like faience vessels and gold. Luxuries are found mostly in large settlements. Notice that the sorting is the historian's own choice of test.

slides.heading: Craft production
slides.body_md: Craft workers used **stones, metals, shell, faience and terracotta**. Chanhudaro was almost wholly devoted to crafts.

visual.alt: Table of Harappan craft materials and what was made from them: stones for beads and seals, metals for tools and ornaments, shell for bangles, and faience and terracotta for small vessels and figurines

slides.narration: Craft workers made beads of carnelian, jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite, tools and ornaments of copper, bronze and gold, bangles of shell, and small vessels of faience and terracotta. Chanhudaro was almost entirely given over to crafts such as bead making, shell cutting, metal working, and making seals and weights.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: spotting a craft centre
slides.body_md: A site shows heaps of chips, stone drills and half-made beads. What do you conclude, and what do you check?
bullets: Step 1 — List the **four traces**: raw material, tools, unfinished objects, waste.
Step 2 — Conclude: a **likely workshop**.
Step 3 — Check: are **finished goods** found elsewhere?
Step 4 — State the limit: who bought the goods is not known.

visual.alt: Flow of evidence for a craft centre: raw material, tools, unfinished objects and waste together point to a likely workshop
visual.caption: Four traces of work

slides.narration: Craft centres are identified from four traces: raw material, tools, unfinished objects and waste. A site with chips, drills and half made beads is very likely a workshop. Then ask where the finished goods were found, since that shows trade. And remember the limit: the traces show who made the goods, not who bought them.

slides.heading: Getting the materials
slides.body_md: Settlements near sources, and **expeditions** to far regions.

rows: Lothal, near the sources around Bharuch
Khetri region of Rajasthan; also Oman

visual.alt: Table of the sources of materials: shell from Nageshwar and Balakot, lapis lazuli near Shortughai, carnelian near Lothal, steatite from south Rajasthan and north Gujarat, copper from the Khetri region and Oman, and gold probably from south India
visual.caption: Where the materials came from

slides.narration: Some materials lay close to settlements, such as shell near Nageshwar and Balakot and lapis lazuli near Shortughai. Lothal lay near carnelian sources, and steatite came from south Rajasthan and north Gujarat. For copper, parties went to the Khetri region of Rajasthan, and gold probably came from south India.

slides.heading: Beyond the subcontinent
slides.body_md: Mesopotamian texts name **Meluhha**, probably the Harappan region. A Harappan jar was found in **Oman**.

visual.alt: Table of distant contacts: Meluhha, probably the Harappan region; Dilmun, Bahrain; Magan, probably Oman; and a Harappan jar found in Oman as evidence of contact across the sea

slides.narration: Mesopotamian texts name three distant lands. Dilmun is linked with Bahrain and Magan probably with Oman. Meluhha is thought to be the Harappan region, because the goods listed for it, such as carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper and gold, match Harappan products. A Harappan jar found in Oman and seals showing boats suggest voyages by sea.

slides.heading: Quick check: a source of lapis lazuli
slides.body_md: Which Harappan settlement lay close to a source of lapis lazuli?
slides.narration: It lay far to the north-west of the subcontinent.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: weighing evidence
slides.body_md: Claim: *Luxury objects show that Harappan society had ranks.* Weigh it.
bullets: Step 1 — **For:** luxuries cluster in large settlements; a few graves hold jewellery.
Step 2 — **Against:** digging has been uneven; most graves are plain.
Step 3 — Note that **luxury** is the historian's label.
Step 4 — Conclude: some difference is **likely**, ranks are **not proven**.

rows: Luxuries are mostly in large settlements

visual.alt: Table weighing the claim that luxuries show social ranks: for, luxuries are mostly in large settlements and a few graves hold jewellery; against, digging has been uneven and most graves are plain

slides.narration: To weigh a claim, set out evidence on both sides. For the claim that luxuries show ranks, we can note that luxuries cluster in large settlements and a few graves hold jewellery. Against it, digging has been uneven and most graves are plain. Finish with a balanced conclusion: some difference is likely, but ranks are not proven.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. The Harappan world had Early, Mature and Late phases. People ate wheat, barley and pulses, kept cattle and other animals, and used ploughs, canals and reservoirs. Mohenjodaro was planned, with a Citadel, a Lower Town, standard bricks and drains. Burials and luxuries hint at social differences. Craft centres made goods from materials found near and far.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: The Citadel was **smaller and higher**, to the **west**.
Wheat and barley were staples; rice only **rarely**.
Graves **hint** at difference; do not write that they prove kings.
Identify a craft centre by **four traces**.
Harappan craftspeople did **not** use iron.

rows: It was smaller and higher, to the west
Wheat and barley; rice only rarely
They hint at differences; no proof of rulers
Copper, bronze and gold; iron came later

visual.alt: Table of exam mistakes and corrections: the Citadel was smaller and higher to the west; wheat and barley, not rice, were staples; graves do not prove kings; and Harappan craftspeople did not use iron

slides.narration: A few tips. The Citadel was smaller and higher, to the west. Wheat and barley were staples and rice was rare. Graves hint at difference but do not prove kings. Remember the four traces of a craft centre. And do not write iron among Harappan materials, because it came into use much later.

decks.title: Bricks, Beads and Bones — Part 2: Seals, Rulers, Decline and Discovery
goals: Explain the use of seals, script and weights
Present the debate on Harappan authority fairly
Evaluate explanations for the end of the cities
Trace the discovery from Cunningham to Wheeler and read a report as a source

slides.heading: Seals, Rulers, Decline and Discovery
slides.body_md: Part 2: what **seals, script and weights** show, who may have held **authority**, how the cities ended, and how they were **found**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: seals, script and weights, the debate on authority, the end of the cities, and discovery with source-based practice
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we look at seals, script and weights, which show how goods were marked and measured. We ask who may have held authority, which is a real debate. We examine explanations for the end of the cities, and we follow the discovery from Cunningham to Wheeler. At the end, we practise reading an archaeological report.

slides.heading: Seals
slides.body_md: Seals were mostly carved from **steatite**, with **animal motifs and signs**.

rows: Marking goods and bundles in long-distance exchange
Clay sealings, sometimes with cord marks

visual.alt: Table of seal features: mostly steatite, animal motifs and signs, used to mark goods in long-distance exchange, with clay sealings as evidence

slides.narration: Seals were mostly made of steatite, a soft stone that is easy to carve. They show animals and a short row of signs. When pressed into clay, a seal left an impression, which archaeologists call a sealing. Sealings found with cord marks suggest that seals were used to mark goods sent over long distances.

slides.heading: How a sealed bundle worked

visual.alt: Flow showing how a sealed bundle probably worked: goods tied, clay fixed on the cord, seal pressed in, bundle travels, and the impression marks the sender
visual.caption: Seal, sealing, bundle

slides.narration: This is the probable sequence. Goods were tied in a bundle with a cord. A lump of clay was fixed on the cord and a seal was pressed into it. The bundle then travelled, and the impression marked the sender and showed that the bundle had not been opened. We infer this from finds, because no Harappan writing explains it.

slides.heading: The script
slides.body_md: The script has about **375 to 400 signs**, is **not alphabetic**, and is **undeciphered**.

rows: Too many for one sign per sound
Signs may stand for words or syllables
Mostly right to left on seals

visual.alt: Table of script facts: about 375 to 400 signs, not alphabetic, mostly right to left on seals, and still undeciphered

slides.narration: The Harappan script has about three hundred seventy five to four hundred signs, which is too many for one sign to stand for one sound. It is not alphabetic. On seals it is mostly written from right to left. Because it is still undeciphered, we do not know the language or what the messages said.

slides.heading: Quick check: seal stone
slides.body_md: Most Harappan seals were carved from a soft stone called ___.
slides.narration: The stone is soft and easy to carve.

slides.heading: Weights
slides.body_md: Weights were of **chert**, usually **cubical**, with no marks. Lower values **doubled**; higher ones were **decimal**.

visual.alt: Table of weight features: chert, usually cubical and unmarked, with lower values doubling and higher values decimal

slides.narration: Weights were made of chert and were usually cubical, with no markings. The lower values doubled each time, as in one, two, four, eight, sixteen and thirty two. The higher values followed a decimal pattern. Such a system suggests careful and consistent measuring, probably in trade and in crafts such as jewellery.

slides.heading: Signs of organisation

visual.alt: Flow of signs of organisation: standard bricks, planned towns, uniform weights and seals on goods lead to the question of who coordinated them
visual.caption: Signs of coordination

slides.narration: Standard bricks, planned towns, uniform weights and seals on goods all point to organisation over a wide area. That raises a question that the evidence cannot settle easily: who coordinated all this? Planning shows that decisions were made. It does not by itself tell us whether the decision makers were kings, councils or others.

slides.heading: Who held authority?
slides.body_md: Three views: **no rulers**, **several rulers**, **one state**. A stone statue called the **priest-king** is a label, not proof.

rows: Society had no distinct ruling group
Each centre had its own ruler
A single authority over the whole region
No palace or royal burial confirmed

visual.alt: Table of three views of Harappan rule: no rulers, several rulers and one state, each with its idea and its difficulty
visual.caption: A debate, not a settled fact

slides.narration: Historians have offered three views. Some say there were no distinct rulers. Others say each major centre had its own ruler. A third view says one state ruled the whole region. No palace or royal burial has been confirmed. The name priest-king, given to a stone statue, is only the archaeologists' label and does not prove who ruled.

slides.heading: Quick check: a palace?
slides.body_md: True or false? Excavations have confirmed a palace and a royal burial at Mohenjodaro.
slides.narration: Think about why the question of rulers is still debated.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: weighing three views
slides.body_md: Question: *Assess which view of Harappan rule the evidence supports best.*
bullets: Step 1 — State the **evidence** of coordination.
Step 2 — Give each **view** with its limit.
Step 3 — Weigh them: which explains **uniformity** best?
Step 4 — Conclude, and say what is **not proven**.

rows: Evidence of complex decisions: bricks, planning, weights
View one: no rulers, with its limit
View two: several rulers, with its limit
View three: one state, with its limit
Your judgement: none proven, which is best supported

visual.alt: Table planning a 5-mark assessment of views of rule: evidence of complex decisions, then each of the three views with its limit, then a reasoned judgement

slides.narration: For an assessment question, start with the evidence that decisions were made: bricks, planning and weights. Then give each of the three views with its limit. Weigh them by asking which best explains the uniformity over a wide area. End with your judgement and say clearly what is not proven, since the debate remains open.

slides.heading: The end of the cities
slides.body_md: By about **1800 BCE** most mature sites in Cholistan and nearby areas were abandoned. Explanations vary; **none is proven**.

visual.alt: Table of explanations for the end of the cities: climatic change, deforestation and overuse of land, excessive floods, and shifting or drying rivers, each with a limit
visual.caption: No single cause proven

slides.narration: By about eighteen hundred BCE most mature sites in regions such as Cholistan were abandoned, and people moved to new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. Explanations include climatic change, deforestation, excessive floods, shifting or drying rivers and overuse of the land. Each has limits, and no single cause is proven.

slides.heading: The invasion idea
columns: **The old claim:** invaders destroyed the cities, as shown by skeletons at Mohenjodaro.
**The problems:** no layer of destruction across sites; George Dales showed that the skeletons do not show one event.

rows: No layer of destruction across the sites
Skeletons at Mohenjodaro show a massacre
Dales showed they do not show one event
Seals and weights faded; people moved on

visual.alt: Table of the invasion claim and its problems: no layer of destruction, the Mohenjodaro skeletons do not show a single event, and change looks gradual

slides.narration: An older view said that invaders destroyed the cities. Skeletons found at Mohenjodaro were cited as proof. But there is no layer of destruction across the sites, and George Dales showed that those skeletons do not point to a single violent event. Most historians now see gradual change, not conquest, as better supported.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the layers
slides.body_md: A lower layer has seals and cubical weights; the upper layer has only coarse pottery. How are they dated?
slides.narration: Think about which phase had seals and weights.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: dating by layers
slides.body_md: A trench shows three layers. Date each layer and list the order from oldest to newest.
bullets: Step 1 — Note the **finds** in each layer.
Step 2 — Match them to **phases**: seals and weights mean Mature.
Step 3 — Remember: **lower** layers are usually **older**.
Step 4 — Write: Early, Mature, Late.

visual.alt: Table of three layers in an imagined trench: top with coarse pottery and no seals, Late Harappan; middle with seals, weights and drilled beads, Mature Harappan; bottom with plain pottery and no seals, Early Harappan

slides.narration: To date layers, first note what each layer contains. Seals, cubical weights and drilled beads mean the Mature phase. Plain pottery without seals below it suggests the Early phase, and coarse pottery without seals above it suggests the Late phase. Lower layers are usually older, so the order from oldest to newest is Early, Mature, Late.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading an archaeological report
slides.body_md: A report says: *Room 4 held forty bead blanks, and it was the workshop of a bead-makers' guild.* Analyse it.
bullets: Step 1 — Note **who** wrote it and **when**.
Step 2 — Separate **what was found** (forty blanks) and **where**.
Step 3 — Mark the **inference**: a guild.
Step 4 — State what **cannot be said**: who organised the work.

visual.caption: Four steps for a source question

slides.narration: When reading a report, first note who wrote it and when. Then separate what was found and where from what the author concludes. Forty bead blanks in a room is an observation. A bead makers guild is an inference. Finish by saying what cannot be known from the report, such as who organised the work or who bought the beads.

slides.heading: Interpreting objects with care
slides.body_md: Readings such as a **mother goddess** rest on **analogy**. They are not proven.

rows: Analogy with later practice; context needed
An early form of a later god

visual.alt: Table of interpretations: female figurines read as a mother goddess and a seal with a seated figure read as an early form of a later god, each with the caution that analogy and resemblance are not proof

slides.narration: Archaeologists sometimes read religious meaning into objects. Some female figurines are called mother goddesses, and a seal with a seated figure has been compared with a later god. These readings borrow from later practice and rest on resemblance. Without context such as find spots and associated objects, they remain interpretations, not facts.

Most mature sites were abandoned by about eighteen hundred BCE, and no single cause is proven. Cunningham, Sahni, Banerji, Marshall and Wheeler shaped the discovery, and stratigraphy made the record reliable.

sections.heading: 1. Phases and subsistence
sections.body_md:
The **Mature Harappan** phase lasted from about **2600 to 1900 BCE**. **Early Harappan** cultures came before it and **Late Harappan** cultures followed. The civilisation takes its name from **Harappa**, the first site found.

**Food:** wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame; millets in Gujarat; rice only rarely. Bones show cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig, with wild animals and fish.

**Farming evidence:** terracotta plough models (Cholistan, Banawali), the ploughed field at Kalibangan with furrows at right angles (perhaps two crops together), canal traces at Shortughai, reservoirs at Dholavira, and wells.

sections.heading: 2. Planning at Mohenjodaro
sections.body_md:
- **Two parts:** a smaller, higher **Citadel** to the west on mud-brick platforms, and a larger, lower, walled **Lower Town** to the east.
- **Planned first:** platforms were laid before building, and **covered drains** were laid out before houses.
- **Bricks:** standard ratio **4:2:1** at sites far apart.
- **Houses:** around courtyards, no ground-floor windows on the street wall, bathing rooms, wells.
- **Public structures:** the **Great Bath**, a tank made watertight, and the **warehouse**, once called the granary. Both names carry interpretations.

sections.heading: 3. Social differences
sections.body_md:
Historians look for differences in **burials** and **artefacts**. Most burials are pits, some with pottery and ornaments, and a few with jewellery or a copper mirror. Lavish tombs of rulers have not been found.

Artefacts are sorted into **utilitarian** objects (daily needs, common materials) and **luxuries** (rare materials or costly methods). Luxuries are found mostly in large settlements.

**Cautions:** beliefs about death shape graves; luxury is the historian's label; the pattern may reflect where digging was done.

sections.heading: 4. Craft production and procurement
sections.body_md:
**Materials:** carnelian, jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite; copper, bronze and gold; shell; faience; terracotta. **Chanhudaro** was almost wholly devoted to craft: beads, shell objects, metal-working, seals and weights.

**Identifying a centre:** raw material, tools, unfinished objects and waste.

**Procurement:** settlements near sources (Nageshwar and Balakot for shell, Shortughai for lapis lazuli, Lothal near carnelian); steatite from south Rajasthan and north Gujarat; **expeditions** to the Khetri region for copper and to south India for gold. **Distant lands:** copper from Oman; Mesopotamian texts name Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan and **Meluhha**, probably the Harappan region.

key_terms.definition_md: A material made by firing powdered sand or silica with colouring and a binder.
The ways of obtaining raw materials, near and far.

sections.heading: 5. Seals, script, weights and authority
sections.body_md:
**Seals** were mostly of steatite, with animal motifs and signs, and were pressed into clay to mark goods. The **script** has about 375 to 400 signs, is not alphabetic, runs mostly right to left on seals and is **undeciphered**. **Weights** were of chert, usually cubical and unmarked, with doubled lower values and decimal higher ones.

**Authority:** planning and uniformity show complex decisions, but no palace or royal burial is confirmed. Three views: **no rulers**, **several rulers**, **one state**. The statue called the **priest-king** is a label by archaeologists.

key_terms.definition_md: A lump of clay carrying the impression of a seal.
Not yet read, so its language and messages are unknown.

sections.heading: 6. The end of the civilisation
sections.body_md:
By about **1800 BCE** most mature sites in regions such as Cholistan were abandoned, and people spread to new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. In the **Late Harappan** phase seals, writing, standard weights and specialised beads faded and life became more rural.

**Explanations:** climatic change, deforestation, excessive floods, shifting or drying rivers, overuse of the land. **No single cause is proven.** The idea of an **invasion** is not supported: there is no layer of destruction, and George Dales showed that the Mohenjodaro skeletons do not show a single massacre.

key_terms.definition_md: The phase after c. 1900 BCE, with no seals, standard weights or script.
Digging and recording layer by layer, so that finds keep their order and context.

sections.heading: 7. Discovery, interpretation and sources
sections.body_md:
**Alexander Cunningham** began work for the Survey in 1861 and later became its first Director-General; he was interested in the Early Historic period and in Chinese pilgrims' accounts; a Harappan seal given to him was not understood. **Daya Ram Sahni** found seals at Harappa (1921), **Rakhal Das Banerji** at Mohenjodaro (1922), and **John Marshall** announced a new civilisation in 1924. Marshall dug in uniform horizontal units; **R. E. M. Wheeler** (Director-General from 1944) followed the layers. After 1947 many sites were found in India, such as Kalibangan, Lothal, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira.

**Interpretation:** readings such as a mother goddess rest on analogy and need context.

**Reading a report:** note author and date, separate observation from inference, and say what cannot be concluded.

key_terms.definition_md: Where and with what an object was found; it tells how the object was used.
A conclusion drawn from evidence, as distinct from what was directly observed.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that the Citadel was lower, or placing it to the east.
- Naming rice as the staple or iron among Harappan materials.
- Treating the **priest-king** or a **mother goddess** as proven.
- Giving a single cause for the end of the cities, or writing that invaders destroyed them.
- Mixing up Marshall (flat units) and Wheeler (layers).
- In source questions, copying a sentence when asked to explain, or stating an inference as a fact.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points, or a point and a reason (30–50 words).
- 3 marks: three distinct points (50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five headed points (80–120 words); assessment questions need evidence on both sides and a judgement.
- Source questions (4 marks): part (a) and (b) one mark each, part (c) two marks with an internal choice.

**Sources in SOYL practice** are imagined documents or SOYL summaries written for practice; the board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: The mature phase of the Harappan civilisation is dated to roughly

options.text_md: 600 to 300 BCE
300 BCE to 200 CE

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 2600 to 1900 BCE. Cultures that came before it are called Early Harappan and those that followed Late Harappan; the dates in the other options belong to much later periods of Indian history.

questions.stem_md: Plant remains from Harappan sites show that people grew and ate

options.text_md: maize, potato, tomato and chilli
tea, coffee and rubber
oats, rye and grapes
wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame. Grains and pulses of the Old World were the staples, with millets at some Gujarat sites and rice only rarely. Maize, potato, tomato and chilli came to India from the Americas many centuries later.

questions.stem_md: Archaeologists uncovered a ploughed field of the Harappan period at Kalibangan, with two sets of furrows cutting each other at right angles. Which statement about this evidence is most careful?

options.text_md: It may mean that two crops were sown together, but the furrows alone do not prove it
It proves that the Harappans used iron ploughs
It shows that the field was watered by a canal from a reservoir
It shows that the field belonged to a ruler of the city

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It may mean that two crops were sown together, but the furrows alone do not prove it. A pattern in the soil is an observation; the idea of mixed cropping is an inference that needs support, such as preserved seeds. Nothing in the furrows tells us about metals, canals or ownership.

questions.stem_md: Compared with the Lower Town at Mohenjodaro, the Citadel was

options.text_md: larger, built at the lowest level and lying to the east
a separate town many kilometres away
smaller, built higher on mud-brick platforms and lying to the west
made only of wood and reeds

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** smaller, built higher on mud-brick platforms and lying to the west. The raised western part held the large public structures; the bigger, lower part to its east, also walled, held the houses.

questions.stem_md: At a newly excavated Harappan town, a drain runs straight beneath a lane, and the foundation of the nearest house wall rests on top of the drain's side wall. Judged by the practice at Mohenjodaro, what does this suggest?

options.text_md: The house was built first and the drain was cut later
The town had no drains at all
The drain was planned and laid before the house was built
The house was a public warehouse

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The drain was planned and laid before the house was built. At Mohenjodaro the platforms and drains were set out first and the houses were fitted around them. A wall resting on the drain fits that order of work, although one trench cannot show it for the whole town.

questions.stem_md: Many Mohenjodaro houses had no windows in the ground-floor walls facing the street. Which explanation do historians usually offer?

options.text_md: Rooms opened onto an inner courtyard, which gave privacy from the lane
Windows had not yet been invented
Houses were built only for the ruler's soldiers
Street walls were too thin to carry a window

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Rooms opened onto an inner courtyard, which gave privacy from the lane. Houses were arranged around a courtyard, which supplied light and air, so the street wall could stay blank. This is an interpretation of the plan, not something written down by the builders.

questions.stem_md: A large brick building at Mohenjodaro was once called the granary, and many scholars now prefer the neutral name warehouse. What is the soundest reason for the change?

options.text_md: The building was proved to be a royal palace
Grain was never grown by the Harappans
The building was shown to be a modern construction
The older name assumed a particular use that the surviving remains cannot establish by themselves

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The older name assumed a particular use that the surviving remains cannot establish by themselves. Naming a building by one function goes beyond what bricks and plan can show. The cautious label describes a large store without claiming what exactly was stored. The Harappans did grow grain, and the building is ancient.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Rice was the main staple grain of the Harappan people.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Rice is found only rarely; wheat and barley were far more common, with millets in parts of Gujarat.

questions.stem_md: Bricks at Harappan sites were made in a standard ratio of length to breadth to height of ___ (write it with colons).
questions.solution_md: The ratio 4:2:1 appears at sites far apart, which shows shared practice.

questions.stem_md: Match each Harappan site or region with the evidence of farming or water management found there.

options.text_md: Kalibangan
Shortughai
Dholavira
Cholistan and Banawali

match_right.text_md: A ploughed field with furrows in two directions

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each pairing follows what excavators reported from the site named.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the Citadel and the Lower Town of Mohenjodaro in two points.
questions.solution_md: One point of contrast for each of two features.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The **Citadel** was smaller, lay to the west and stood higher on platforms of mud brick. (2) The **Lower Town** was larger and lower, lay to its east, was also walled, and held the houses laid out in blocks.

questions.stem_md: A visitor says the covered drains show only that the Harappans liked cleanliness. What else can a historian infer from the drains? Give two inferences.
questions.solution_md: Two inferences: advance planning and coordination beyond the household.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The drains were **laid out before the houses**, so decisions about the layout were taken **before building began**, which shows planning. (2) Channels from many houses joined a **shared system**, so someone must have **coordinated and maintained** it beyond single households.

marking_scheme.step: Inference of planning, from the order of work
Inference of coordination, from the shared system

questions.stem_md: An imagined site yields charred barley and sesame seeds, cattle and fish bones and a terracotta plough model, but no rice. What can a historian conclude about subsistence here, and what is one limit of this evidence?
questions.solution_md: Conclusions about crops and animals, and a limit about survival and sampling.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The people **grew grain and oil-seed crops**, barley and sesame, and probably used the **plough**. (2) They **kept cattle and also ate fish**, so food came from herding and fishing as well as farming. (3) **Limit:** the lack of rice at one site does not show that rice was unknown elsewhere, and seeds and bones show only what happened to survive.

questions.stem_md: Describe the planning of the settlement at Mohenjodaro.
questions.solution_md: Layout, advance planning, bricks, drainage and houses each earn a mark.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Two parts:** a smaller, higher **Citadel** to the west and a larger, lower **Lower Town**, both walled.
2. **Platforms first:** mud-brick platforms were laid before building began, so the layout was decided beforehand.
3. **Standard bricks:** bricks followed one ratio of 4:2:1.
4. **Drains:** covered drains were planned before the houses and ran along the lanes.
5. **Houses:** built around courtyards, with blank street walls, private bathrooms and often a well.
The Great Bath and the large warehouse were public structures on the Citadel.

marking_scheme.step: Houses with courtyards and other public structures

questions.stem_md: Read the source from the imagined field diary of an excavation assistant and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Any one feature of the drain from the first part of the passage.

**(b)** Find the sentence about foundations and use the order of building.

**(c) (i)** Two inferences, each resting on a detail of the diary.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two reasons about sampling and place.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The lane had a **brick-lined drain, covered with flat bricks**, which small **channels from the houses** joined.

**(b)** The last sentence, about the drain's foundation lying **beneath the lowest course of the house wall**: the wall was raised after the drain was in place.

**(c) (i)** (1) The **same brick size** in houses two lanes apart suggests **shared standards** and a workforce or authority that enforced them. (2) A drain **capped and joined by house channels** suggests a **common system** that someone maintained, not each family acting alone.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) **One house is a small sample**; other houses may differ in size, plan or wealth. (2) The diary comes from one **lane in one trench** of one city, so it cannot show how houses looked in other areas or at other sites.

questions.passage_md:
**Field diary of an excavation assistant (imagined), Lower Town, cool season**

Day 12. We cleared the lane in Trench C down to its old street level. It is straight and wide enough for two bullock carts. Along its edge runs a drain lined with brick and capped with flat bricks, and every few steps a small channel from a house wall joins it. The house on the left has no opening at all on the lane side; its door is on a narrower side lane. Inside, bricks of one size surround a square courtyard, with a small bathing room in one corner. The mason working with us says that the bricks match those of a house two lanes away. Today I found the drain's foundation resting on the lane's first surface, beneath the lowest course of the house wall.

children.stem_md: Name one feature of the lane that shows that drainage was organised.
children.solution_md: Any one feature of the drain from the first part of the passage.

answer.model_answer_md: The lane had a **brick-lined drain, covered with flat bricks**, which small **channels from the houses** joined.

children.stem_md: Which sentence of the diary supports the view that the drains were laid before the houses were built? Say in one line why.
children.solution_md: Find the sentence about foundations and use the order of building.

answer.model_answer_md: The last sentence, about the drain's foundation lying **beneath the lowest course of the house wall**: the wall was raised after the drain was in place.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): What can historians infer from this diary about how the settlement was organised? Give two inferences that the diary does not state in so many words.
children.solution_md: Two inferences, each resting on a detail of the diary.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The **same brick size** in houses two lanes apart suggests **shared standards** and a workforce or authority that enforced them. (2) A drain **capped and joined by house channels** suggests a **common system** that someone maintained, not each family acting alone.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The assistant describes only one house. Why should historians be careful before claiming that all Harappan houses were like it? Give two reasons.
alternatives.solution_md: Two reasons about sampling and place.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **One house is a small sample**; other houses may differ in size, plan or wealth. (2) The diary comes from one **lane in one trench** of one city, so it cannot show how houses looked in other areas or at other sites.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined cemetery, three pit burials hold pottery and a few ornaments, one holds a copper mirror and shell bangles, and two hold nothing. What is the most careful use of this evidence?

options.text_md: It proves that the buried people ruled the city
The differences may point to social differences, but more evidence would be needed before concluding that
It proves that everyone in the community was equal
It cannot be used by historians at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The differences may point to social differences, but more evidence would be needed before concluding that. Different goods in graves are a clue to differing status, yet beliefs about death, family choice and chance of survival also matter. Neither a firm claim of rulers nor of equality follows from six graves.

questions.stem_md: A student says that faience vessels count as luxuries because they are found mostly in big cities. What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.text_md: Whether an object is a luxury depends on its rare material or costly making, not on where it is found; the distribution is a separate observation
Faience vessels were found in small villages in equal numbers
Luxuries are never found in cities
Faience was a common material used for cooking pots

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Whether an object is a luxury depends on its rare material or costly making, not on where it is found; the distribution is a separate observation. The test for a luxury is about the material and the effort of making. Where objects turn up is a different matter, which may or may not point to unequal access.

questions.stem_md: Costly objects such as faience vessels are found mostly in large settlements like Mohenjodaro and Harappa and only rarely in small ones. Which interpretation fits the evidence best?

options.text_md: Small settlements never traded with large ones
Access to such objects may have differed between places, though the pattern may also reflect where excavation has been done
Large settlements were ruled by kings and small ones were not
Faience was banned in villages by law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Access to such objects may have differed between places, though the pattern may also reflect where excavation has been done. A pattern in finds can show real unevenness, yet it can also come from uneven digging. A claim about kings or laws goes far beyond the distribution itself.

questions.stem_md: Which of these materials was not used by Harappan craftspeople?

options.text_md: Carnelian
Shell
Iron
Copper

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Iron. Harappan metalwork used copper, bronze and gold; iron came into use in the subcontinent much later.

questions.stem_md: A dig yields piles of cut shell, stone saws and many half-cut bangles in a room, but almost no finished bangles. What is the best reading?

options.text_md: The room was a royal treasury
The bangles were never meant to be worn
Shell was unknown to the Harappans
The room was probably a workshop, and finished bangles were likely taken elsewhere

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The room was probably a workshop, and finished bangles were likely taken elsewhere. Raw material, tools and unfinished pieces mark a place of work. Finished goods are carried away to be used or exchanged, which explains why few remain at the workshop.

questions.stem_md: Which Harappan settlement lay close to a source of lapis lazuli?

options.text_md: Chanhudaro
Dholavira
Kalibangan
Shortughai

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Shortughai. Shortughai, in Afghanistan, was positioned near the source of the blue stone, which then travelled to other Harappan towns.

questions.stem_md: Which further finding would most strengthen the view that Meluhha was the Harappan region?

options.text_md: More Mesopotamian texts that also name Dilmun
Lapis lazuli used in later Indian jewellery
Seals of the Harappan type found at Mesopotamian sites
Gold found in Egyptian tombs

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Seals of the Harappan type found at Mesopotamian sites. Harappan-type objects at Mesopotamian sites would show direct contact between the two regions. The other finds say nothing about where Meluhha lay.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Chanhudaro is regarded by archaeologists as a settlement devoted almost entirely to craft production.

**Reason (R):** Its excavated area yielded traces of bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The workshop traces are exactly the evidence on which the label rests, so the second statement supports the first.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Historians treat grave goods as only partial evidence for social differences among the Harappans.

**Reason (R):** Most Harappan burials were simple pits with few or no goods, and lavish burials of the kind found in some ancient societies have not been found.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Because the burials show only modest and uneven contrasts, grave goods alone cannot establish a firm social hierarchy, which is why the second statement explains the first.

questions.stem_md: Mesopotamian texts name a distant land called ___ as a source of carnelian and lapis lazuli; it was probably the Harappan region.
questions.solution_md: The land is Meluhha, while Dilmun and Magan are linked with Bahrain and Oman.

questions.stem_md: Match each place with the material that its location gave access to.

options.text_md: Shortughai
Nageshwar and Balakot
Lothal
Khetri region of Rajasthan

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each setting was close to, or an expedition target for, the material named.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Pictures of ships and boats on Harappan seals are one clue that sea voyages were likely.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** They hint at travel by water; other evidence, such as a Harappan jar in Oman, points the same way.

questions.stem_md: How do archaeologists sort artefacts into utilitarian objects and luxuries? Give one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Criterion and example for each class.

answer.model_answer_md: **Utilitarian** objects serve daily needs and are made of common materials, such as a **grinding slab** or a cooking pot. **Luxuries** are made of rare materials or by costly methods and are not needed for daily life, such as a **faience vessel** or gold ornament.

questions.stem_md: A site yields many finished beads but no drills, unfinished beads or waste. Why would archaeologists hesitate to call it a craft centre?
questions.solution_md: The reason rests on what marks a workshop and an alternative source of the beads.

answer.model_answer_md: A craft centre is identified by **raw material, tools, unfinished objects and waste**, which show that work was done on the spot. Finished beads alone could have **arrived by trade**, so without those traces the site may simply have used the beads.

marking_scheme.step: Beads could have been brought in

questions.stem_md: An imagined Harappan settlement is found beside a steatite source, with seal-makers' tools in its houses. Explain three ways in which such a location would help the Harappan economy.
questions.solution_md: Supply, workshop and distribution benefits of a site near the material.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Cheap, easy supply** of steatite, which saved long journeys to fetch raw material. (2) A place where **seals could be made close to the stone**, with less waste from carrying unworked blocks. (3) A **supplier for other towns**, so that finished or half-worked seals could travel to distant cities along existing trade routes.

questions.stem_md: Why must historians be careful in using burials and luxury objects to infer social differences? Give three reasons.
questions.solution_md: Three limits on the evidence, none of them a restatement of the burials themselves.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Graves vary only modestly, so **no clear ranks** can be read from them. (2) Luxuries cluster in **large settlements**, but that may reflect **where archaeologists have dug**. (3) What counts as a luxury depends on **historians' own classification**, which may not match how Harappans valued things.

questions.stem_md: To what extent did Harappan craft production depend on distant regions for its raw materials?
questions.solution_md: Near sources, expeditions and distant lands weighed, with a craft-centre example and a conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Near sources:** Nageshwar and Balakot (shell), Shortughai (lapis lazuli) and Lothal (carnelian) lay close to their materials, and steatite came from south Rajasthan and north Gujarat.
2. **Expeditions:** parties went to the Khetri region for copper and to south India for gold, so some needs were met by organised journeys.
3. **Distant lands:** copper also came from Oman.
4. **Craft centres:** Chanhudaro, given almost wholly to crafts, relied on materials brought to it.
5. **Judgement:** dependence was real but mostly on regions within or beside the Harappan world; distant lands supplied some metal and markets, so it was partial.

questions.stem_md: Read the source from an imagined museum guide's notes and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Read the third and fourth sentences of the passage.

**(b)** Tools found beside waste point to work done there.

**(c) (i)** Two kinds of evidence of exchange that the passage does not supply.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two practical requirements for a craft town far from its raw material.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Chips of shell**, broken carnelian or discarded bead blanks (any one).

**(b)** The beads were **made on the spot**: the town was a **workshop**, not just a place that used beads.

**(c) (i)** (1) **Seals or clay sealings** at the town or in the cities, which would show goods being marked and sent. (2) **Weights** and the **distribution of the same bead types** in other places, which would show standard measures and routes of exchange.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) A **dependable way to bring the stone in bulk**, such as traders, carriers or organised expeditions. (2) **Links with other settlements** that would buy the finished beads, so that the cost of getting the raw stone was repaid.

questions.passage_md:
**Museum guide's notes on a craft town (imagined)**

Visitors often ask why this small town had no grand hall or large store. The answer lies in the workshop lanes. Nearly every house in the excavated area had heaps of waste: chips of shell, broken carnelian and discarded bead blanks. Drills of hard stone, grinding slabs and small furnaces lay beside them. The nearest source of carnelian is far away, so the stone must have arrived in bulk, probably carried by traders or by the workers themselves. Finished beads from this town have turned up in larger cities, but we do not yet know who paid for them or how they were exchanged.

children.solution_md: Read the third and fourth sentences of the passage.

answer.model_answer_md: **Chips of shell**, broken carnelian or discarded bead blanks (any one).

children.stem_md: The drills, grinding slabs and furnaces lay beside the waste. What do they tell us about where the beads were made?
children.solution_md: Tools found beside waste point to work done there.

answer.model_answer_md: The beads were **made on the spot**: the town was a **workshop**, not just a place that used beads.

marking_scheme.step: Made on the spot, a workshop

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): The guide says that we do not know how the beads were exchanged. Suggest two kinds of evidence archaeologists could look for to find out.
children.solution_md: Two kinds of evidence of exchange that the passage does not supply.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Seals or clay sealings** at the town or in the cities, which would show goods being marked and sent. (2) **Weights** and the **distribution of the same bead types** in other places, which would show standard measures and routes of exchange.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The town was far from its carnelian source. Give two things that its craftspeople would have needed to keep working.
alternatives.solution_md: Two practical requirements for a craft town far from its raw material.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) A **dependable way to bring the stone in bulk**, such as traders, carriers or organised expeditions. (2) **Links with other settlements** that would buy the finished beads, so that the cost of getting the raw stone was repaid.

questions.stem_md: Why does a sealing found in a distant storeroom tell historians more about exchange than a seal found in a house?

options.text_md: A sealing is made of a harder stone than a seal
A sealing shows that the seal was actually pressed on goods that moved, whereas a seal shows only that someone held it
A sealing carries a message that has been deciphered
A sealing proves that the storeroom belonged to a ruler

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A sealing shows that the seal was actually pressed on goods that moved, whereas a seal shows only that someone held it. The impression is a trace of use on goods, and its place of discovery shows where they ended up. A seal alone gives no sign of movement. Nothing here is deciphered or tied to a ruler.

questions.stem_md: Inscriptions on most Harappan seals are read from

options.text_md: right to left
left to right
top to bottom
the centre outwards in a spiral

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** right to left. Scholars have worked out the direction even though the script itself is still unread.

questions.stem_md: An imagined set of Harappan weights has the values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64, and then 640, 6,400 and 64,000. Which statement matches the pattern of Harappan weights?

options.text_md: All values follow a decimal pattern
The smaller values double each time, and the larger values follow a decimal pattern
All values double each time without any change
The values follow no pattern at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The smaller values double each time, and the larger values follow a decimal pattern. Check the two stretches separately: the first seven values double each time, and each of the last three is ten times the one before. Doubling first and decimal later is how Harappan weights are described.

questions.stem_md: Archaeologists find a seal with an animal and four signs at one site, and a clay sealing made by an identical seal at a site about 500 km away. What can and cannot be concluded?

options.text_md: The signs name the ruler of both places
The language of the signs is now confirmed
The second site was governed from the first
Goods marked with this seal probably travelled between the two places, but the meaning of the signs stays unknown

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Goods marked with this seal probably travelled between the two places, but the meaning of the signs stays unknown. The matching impression is evidence of movement or contact. Reading the signs or naming rulers would need evidence that the find does not supply, since the script is undeciphered.

questions.stem_md: Which discovery, if it were made, would most weaken the view that the Harappan world formed one state?

options.text_md: Mohenjodaro and Harappa being found to use clearly different standards of bricks and weights
Bricks of the 4:2:1 ratio at distant sites
Seals of one type in many cities
A large warehouse at Mohenjodaro

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Mohenjodaro and Harappa being found to use clearly different standards of bricks and weights. The one-state view leans on uniformity, so evidence of separate standards at the two great centres would cut against it. The other findings fit uniformity or say nothing about it.

questions.stem_md: A student writes: The stone statue called the priest-king proves that Harappan cities were ruled by priests. What is the main flaw in this claim?

options.text_md: The statue was made in Mauryan times
The statue is made of iron
The label is the archaeologists' own guess about a single figure, which cannot show who held power
Harappan cities had no religion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The label is the archaeologists' own guess about a single figure, which cannot show who held power. A name given to an object records an interpretation. One statue with no inscription is not enough to say who governed. The other options state facts that are wrong or unsupported.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Standard weights suggest that exchange in the Harappan world was regulated.

**Reason (R):** Harappan weights were usually cubical, made of chert, and carried no markings.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: One conclusion about movement of goods and one about the limits of identification.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Goods tied with a cord were **sealed in one place and sent** to another, so the storeroom was probably receiving goods. (2) The **design** identified the sender or owner, though the **script cannot be read**, so we cannot say who the sender was.

questions.stem_md: State two features of the Harappan script.
questions.solution_md: Any two features from the set of facts known about the script.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) It is **not alphabetic** and has about **375 to 400 signs**, so one sign did not stand for one sound. (2) It is written mostly **from right to left** on seals and has **not been deciphered**, so its language is unknown.

questions.stem_md: Sets of weights from two Harappan sites about 600 km apart follow the same doubling pattern. State two conclusions historians can reasonably draw, and note one thing the weights cannot show.
questions.solution_md: Two conclusions from the matching pattern and one limit.

answer.model_answer_md: The sites **shared a system of measurement**, which suggests contact or common standards in exchange, and some form of **coordination**. The weights **cannot show who set the standard**, since they carry no marks or writing.

questions.stem_md: Why is it difficult to prove that the Harappan world was ruled by kings? Give three reasons.
questions.solution_md: Three reasons: missing physical evidence, ambiguous evidence of order, and silent writing.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) No **palace** or **king's burial** has been clearly identified. (2) **Planning and uniform artefacts** show coordination, but that could come from one state, several rulers or shared custom. (3) The **script is unread**, so no inscription tells us who held power; names such as priest-king are guesses made by archaeologists.

questions.stem_md: Historians have offered three views of Harappan rule: no rulers, several rulers, or one state. Assess which view the evidence supports best.
questions.solution_md: Evidence, each of the three views weighed, and a reasoned conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Evidence to explain:** planned cities, standard bricks, weights and seals show complex decisions and coordination.
2. **No rulers:** the lack of a confirmed palace or royal burial supports it, but organised work on this scale makes it hard to believe that nobody directed it.
3. **Several rulers:** separate centres such as Mohenjodaro and Harappa may each have had a ruler, as their different layouts hint.
4. **One state:** uniform artefacts and planning over a wide area fit a single authority, yet uniformity may come from shared custom.
5. **Judgement:** none is proven; the one-state view explains uniformity best, while the missing palace and unread script keep the debate open.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined trench the lower layer holds seals, cubical weights and drilled carnelian beads, and the upper layer holds only coarse local pottery. How should the two layers be dated?

options.text_md: The lower layer is Late Harappan and the upper layer is Mature Harappan
Both layers are Early Harappan
The lower layer is Mature Harappan and the upper layer is Late Harappan
Both layers belong to the Mauryan period

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The lower layer is Mature Harappan and the upper layer is Late Harappan. Seals, standard weights and specialised beads belong to the mature phase, whose features fade later; layers also run from older at the bottom to newer at the top.

questions.stem_md: Skeletons are found lying together in one layer at a Harappan site. For historians to read them as victims of a single massacre by invaders, which evidence would be most essential?

options.text_md: That all the bodies date from the same moment, show signs of violent death and lie with a layer of destruction
That most of the bodies are those of adults
That pottery lying near them is finely painted
That the site lies close to a river

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** That all the bodies date from the same moment, show signs of violent death and lie with a layer of destruction. A massacre must be shown by simultaneous death, violence and damage to the settlement. This is the standard on which critics such as George Dales found the Mohenjodaro skeletons wanting.

questions.stem_md: Who was the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India?

options.text_md: John Marshall
R. E. M. Wheeler
Daya Ram Sahni
Alexander Cunningham

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Alexander Cunningham. Cunningham began the Survey's work in 1861; Marshall and Wheeler held the post later.

questions.stem_md: Cunningham was shown a Harappan seal but did not grasp its importance. What does this episode best illustrate about archaeological work?

options.text_md: Seals are never important for history
What scholars recognise in a find depends partly on the periods and questions already in their minds
A find loses value when it is handed over by someone else
Early archaeologists deliberately hid evidence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** What scholars recognise in a find depends partly on the periods and questions already in their minds. His attention was on the Early Historic period and the accounts of Chinese pilgrims, so an older kind of object did not fit his framework. This is a limit of perspective, not of honesty.

questions.stem_md: An old report says a seal and a bead were found at the same depth in a sloping mound dug in flat units. Why can a historian not assume they are of the same age?

options.text_md: On a slope the same depth can cut across different layers, so the two may belong to different periods
Seals and beads are always made at different times
Depth records are never kept in reports
A bead cannot be dated at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** On a slope the same depth can cut across different layers, so the two may belong to different periods. Layers dip along a sloping mound, so a flat unit takes in deposits of different ages at the same depth. Equal depth is therefore weak evidence of equal age.

questions.stem_md: Two seals come from one trench in a mound, one from a high layer and one from a deep layer. Which practice would let the archaeologist record that the deeper seal is probably older?

options.text_md: Digging in equal-depth units across the whole mound
Following and recording each layer separately as the digging proceeds
Putting all finds from the trench in one bag
Leaving out the depth at which each find lay

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Following and recording each layer separately as the digging proceeds. Recording layers keeps the order in which deposits built up, which is the point of stratigraphy, the method followed by R. E. M. Wheeler.

questions.stem_md: Some archaeologists read certain terracotta female figurines as images of a mother goddess. Which is the best evaluation of this reading?

options.text_md: It is proven, since the figurines are female
It is false, since the Harappans had no religion
It is plausible by analogy with later practice but unproven, and needs supporting context such as where the figurines were found
It is irrelevant to history

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is plausible by analogy with later practice but unproven, and needs supporting context such as where the figurines were found. A religious reading of an object borrows from later or other societies, so it needs find-spots and associated objects to be more than a guess. The other options claim certainty either way.

questions.stem_md: A survey records 120 mature Harappan sites in one region and only 20 of the later phase there, but 150 later sites in a neighbouring region with far fewer before. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text_md: The whole population died out
Invaders must have destroyed the first region
Rivers must have dried up in both regions
Many people probably moved to new areas, though the survey alone does not say why

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Many people probably moved to new areas, though the survey alone does not say why. A fall in one place matched by a rise in another points to movement. The cause of the movement, whether climate, rivers or something else, needs separate evidence.

questions.stem_md: An excavation report lists beads, seals and pots but does not say in which layer or room each was found. Which conclusion would be least safe to draw from it?

options.text_md: That beads, seals and pots were all found at the site
That the site was occupied for some time
That the report's authors thought the finds worth recording
That a seal and a bead listed together were used together in one building

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** That a seal and a bead listed together were used together in one building. Without find-spots the link between objects is lost, so only the general presence of types at the site can be stated safely.

questions.stem_md: Which sentence in an excavation report is an inference rather than a direct observation?

options.text_md: The house had six rooms arranged round a courtyard.
A copper mirror lay in one of the graves nearby.
The family in this house were wealthy merchants.
Ash lay on the floor of Room 2.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The family in this house were wealthy merchants. Counting rooms, noting an object and describing ash are observations. The wealth and trade of a family go beyond what such finds can show by themselves.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Historians do not treat any single cause as proven for the end of the mature Harappan cities.

**Reason (R):** Surveys show different patterns in different regions, with some places abandoned while new settlements grew elsewhere.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Uneven patterns across regions are hard to fit to one cause, so the second statement is a reason for the caution stated in the first.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** John Marshall's teams dug Harappan sites by following the natural layers of the mounds.

**Reason (R):** R. E. M. Wheeler later insisted that excavation must follow the layers of a mound.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Marshall worked in uniform horizontal units, so the first statement is false; the second is true and was a response to that practice.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Skeletons found at Mohenjodaro were once used to argue that the city ended in a massacre, but this reading is now doubted.

**Reason (R):** George Dales showed that all those skeletons lay together in one layer along with signs of conquest and fire.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The first statement is accurate. The second reverses what Dales argued, which was that the remains did not add up to evidence of a single violent event.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the Late Harappan phase, seals and standard weights continued to be widely used.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** They faded away, together with the script and specialised bead-making, as life became more rural.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps in the discovery of the Harappan civilisation in chronological order.

options.text_md: Wheeler becomes Director-General
Sahni digs at Harappa and finds seals
Marshall announces a new civilisation
Cunningham begins work in the Archaeological Survey

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). Cunningham started in 1861, Sahni dug at Harappa in 1921, Marshall made his announcement in 1924 and Wheeler took charge in 1944.
